What is Harness, and how does its Contin: Harness is a CD/CI platform that provides deployment strategies (canary, blue-green, rolling), approval workflows, and rollback as built-in, configurable pipeline primitives rather than something you script yourself in Groovy. Where a Jenkins pipeline is imperative code you write to orchestrate a deploy (and canary/rollback logic has to be built and maintained by hand), a Harness pipeline is declarative configuration selecting a deployment strategy from a library of pre-built, tested patterns - trading some flexibility for significantly less custom pipeline code to write and maintain, plus built-in visualization of every deployment's progress and history.
Explain the Harness Delegate - what is i: The Harness Delegate is a lightweight service you run inside your own infrastructure (a Kubernetes Pod, a VM, or a Docker container) that polls Harness's control plane (SaaS or self-managed) for tasks and executes them locally against your actual cloud/cluster resources - your cloud credentials and network access never need to be exposed to or held by Harness's control plane directly. This matters for security and network topology: the Delegate only needs outbound connectivity to Harness, so it works cleanly even in a private VPC/cluster with no inbound access required, and your sensitive infrastructure credentials stay within a component you fully control.
How does Harness implement canary and bl: In Harness, canary and blue-green are selected as a deployment strategy type on a Stage, with the actual traffic-shifting/replica-count steps auto-generated based on the strategy and your Kubernetes manifest - you configure the canary percentage/steps and Harness handles creating the canary workload, shifting traffic (via Service mesh or native K8s Service updates), running verification, and promoting or rolling back. In Jenkins, achieving the same behavior means writing and maintaining the actual kubectl/Helm commands for each phase yourself (or integrating a separate tool like Argo Rollouts) - Harness's value proposition here is turning a pattern that's normally custom pipeline code into reusable, pre-tested configuration.
What is a Harness Pipeline, Stage, and S: A Pipeline is the top-level workflow definition, containing one or more Stages executed in sequence (or in parallel, if configured) - each Stage represents a distinct phase like Build, Deploy to Dev, or Deploy to Prod, and is typed (a Deployment stage, an Approval stage, a Custom/CI stage). Within a Stage, Steps are the individual actions executed in order (e.g. a 'Rollout Deployment' step, a 'Verify' step running health checks, a 'Shell Script' step for custom logic) - this three-level hierarchy (Pipeline > Stage > Step) is what lets Harness visualize and independently retry/debug at a granular level rather than treating a deploy as one opaque script execution.
How does Harness's GitOps module differ: Harness GitOps is actually built on ArgoCD under the hood (it embeds and manages ArgoCD instances/agents), so the core reconciliation engine is the same - the difference is Harness wraps it with a unified UI/API alongside its CD pipelines, centralized multi-cluster GitOps Application management, and the ability to trigger GitOps syncs as steps within a broader Harness pipeline (e.g. a pipeline that builds an image, runs approval, then triggers a GitOps sync as one of its stages) - useful if you want GitOps reconciliation integrated into a single pipeline view rather than operating a separate standalone ArgoCD instance and UI.
How would you migrate a set of Jenkins p: Build/CI logic (compiling code, running tests, building images) maps over fairly directly into Harness CI stages or can continue running in Jenkins with Harness only handling CD - many migrations start there, keeping Jenkins for build and adopting Harness just for deployment orchestration. What needs genuine redesign is any custom deployment logic written as Groovy/shell script in Jenkins (canary steps, approval gates, rollback logic) - these should be re-expressed using Harness's native deployment strategy and approval-stage primitives rather than ported as a giant 'Shell Script' step, since keeping deployment logic as opaque scripts inside Harness forfeits most of the platform's actual value (visualization, built-in strategies, verification).
What is Harness Feature Flags, and how w: Harness Feature Flags is a feature-flagging module letting you deploy code to production behind a flag that's initially off, then gradually enable it for a percentage of users or specific segments independently of the deployment itself - this decouples 'the code is running in production' from 'users can see/use the feature,' so a bad feature can be turned off instantly via the flag (no rollback deployment needed) and a canary-style gradual rollout can happen at the feature level, not just the infrastructure level.
How would you design an approval workflo: Add an Approval stage (or step) positioned between the staging deployment stage and the production deployment stage, configured with specific approver users/groups and optionally auto-approval conditions (e.g. auto-approve if staging verification passed with zero errors, but require manual approval otherwise) - the pipeline pauses at that stage until approved or rejected, with the approval action, approver identity, and timestamp all captured in the pipeline execution history for audit purposes.
What is Harness Cloud Cost Management (C: Harness CCM ingests cloud billing and Kubernetes utilization data to show cost broken down by namespace, workload, team, or label, and surfaces optimization recommendations (rightsizing over-provisioned workloads, identifying idle resources, recommending commitment-based discounts) directly tied to what's actually running - the Kubernetes-aware cost attribution (mapping cloud spend down to individual workloads/namespaces, not just the cluster as a whole) is its main differentiator versus reading raw cloud billing console data alone, which can't attribute shared cluster cost to specific teams/services without this kind of tooling.
What is Harness Chaos Engineering, and h: Harness Chaos Engineering (built on the open-source LitmusChaos project) lets you define and run controlled fault-injection experiments against a system - killing a Pod, injecting network latency, exhausting CPU/memory on a node - to verify your service actually degrades or recovers the way you assume it will, rather than trusting an untested assumption about resilience. You'd design a chaos experiment targeting a specific failure mode you want to validate (e.g. 'does my HPA actually scale out fast enough when a node is killed'), run it in a controlled environment with defined blast-radius limits, and use the observed behavior to fix gaps before a real, uncontrolled version of that failure happens in production.
How does Harness Security Testing Orches: STO adds security scanning (SAST, DAST, SCA/dependency scanning, container image scanning) as native pipeline steps that aggregate results from multiple underlying scanning tools into one unified view with deduplication and severity-based policy gates - rather than each scanner living as a disconnected pipeline step with its own separate report, STO gives one consolidated 'security posture' view per pipeline run and can block promotion if findings exceed a configured severity threshold, the same kind of automated security gate discussed for any mature CI/CD pipeline, just with Harness-native tooling and reporting.
How do Harness Connectors work, and what: A Connector is Harness's abstraction for any external system integration (a Git repo, a Kubernetes cluster, a cloud provider, an artifact registry, a Vault instance) - it stores the connection details and, for the actual credential, either references a Harness-native encrypted secret or delegates to an external secrets manager (Vault, AWS/GCP/Azure secret managers) so the raw credential value can be kept outside Harness's own control plane entirely if required. Connectors are typically configured to route through a Delegate for the actual connection, meaning the credential is used within your infrastructure boundary rather than the credential itself needing to reach out to Harness's SaaS control plane.
How would you troubleshoot a Harness pip: For a stuck pipeline, check the specific step it's stuck on in the execution view first - it's almost always waiting on something identifiable (a pending manual approval, a Delegate that isn't picking up the task, a downstream API call that's hanging) rather than Harness itself being broken. For a disconnected Delegate, check the Delegate Pod/VM's own logs and resource health (a Delegate can silently die from OOM or lose network connectivity to Harness's control plane) - Harness's UI shows Delegate heartbeat status, so confirming the Delegate is actually reachable and healthy is the first diagnostic step before assuming a pipeline-configuration problem.
What is a Harness Environment and Infras: A Service represents what you're deploying (the application, its manifests/Helm chart, its artifact source) independent of where it runs. An Environment represents a logical deployment target (dev, staging, prod) and its associated configuration (environment-specific variable overrides). An Infrastructure Definition specifies the actual concrete target within that environment (a specific Kubernetes cluster/namespace, or cloud account/region) - this three-way separation lets the same Service definition be deployed to multiple Environments/Infrastructure Definitions without duplicating the deployment logic itself, only the environment-specific configuration differing per target.
How would you implement a rollback strat: Configure a Verify step (using Harness's built-in verification against Prometheus/Datadog/CloudWatch metrics, or a custom health check) immediately after the deploy step, with a defined failure condition - if verification fails, the pipeline's built-in rollback behavior automatically reverts to the last successful deployment's state (for Kubernetes, this is effectively re-applying the previous manifest/revision) without needing custom rollback scripting, since rollback-on-failed-verification is a native pipeline behavior tied to the deployment strategy you selected, not something you have to author yourself.
How does Harness handle secrets manageme: Harness has its own built-in encrypted secrets store for simple cases (a value entered once, encrypted at rest, referenced by name in pipelines) - convenient but means Harness's control plane is now a place a secret value transits through. For more sensitive secrets or an org already standardized on centralized secrets management, Harness integrates with external providers (Vault, AWS/GCP/Azure secret managers) via a Secret Manager connector, so Harness only stores a reference/path and fetches the actual value at execution time through the Delegate - keeping the real secret value within your own infrastructure boundary rather than Harness's SaaS control plane, which is generally the preferred pattern for anything genuinely sensitive.
When would you choose Harness over Jenki: Choose Harness when you want one unified platform covering CI, CD, GitOps, feature flags, cost management, and security scanning with a consistent UI and less integration glue code to build and maintain yourself - a meaningful win for a smaller platform team without capacity to operate and integrate several separate open-source tools. The tradeoff is vendor lock-in and cost (Harness is a commercial product with real licensing cost at scale) versus the separate-tools approach, which is more composable and avoids lock-in but requires the team to build and maintain the integration glue (dashboards, cross-tool visibility, custom canary logic) themselves - the decision usually comes down to whether the platform team's time is better spent operating Harness or building/maintaining that glue code.
How would you set up multi-environment p: Define one Pipeline with sequential Stages per environment (Deploy to Dev, Deploy to Staging, Deploy to Prod), each referencing the same Service but a different Environment/Infrastructure Definition - Dev auto-deploys with no gate, Staging deploys automatically but with a Verify step gating progression, and Prod is preceded by an Approval stage requiring specific approvers plus its own Verify/rollback configuration. This structure means promotion through environments is the pipeline naturally progressing stage by stage, with each environment's specific risk tolerance expressed as that stage's own gates rather than needing separate, disconnected pipelines per environment.
